background: In July 2024, the Indian stock brokerage firm Angel One confirmed that data leaked online related to a breach that occurred in April 2023 . The leaked data included 7.9M user records containing 6.8M unique email addresses, along with names, physical addresses, phone numbers, bank account numbers, Permanent Account Numbers (PANs) and portfolio holdings. Angel One emphasised that the breach "has no impact on client securities, funds, or credentials".
how: The published account does not explain the exact way the data was obtained.
outcome: Have I Been Pwned lists 6,765,054 email addresses in this breach record. An address total measures the source record's coverage.
The reported exposed data includes Bank account numbers, Dates of birth, Email addresses, Financial investments, Government issued IDs, Names, Phone numbers, Physical addresses.
editorial: Angel One's statement that the breach "has no impact on client securities, funds, or credentials" is probably accurate as far as it goes, and it misses the point. Nobody needs your trading password to misuse this data. The set pairs names, phone numbers and addresses with bank account numbers, PANs and portfolio holdings, which is a complete brief for an investment scam.

India's stock-market fraud of the moment is the fake trading group: a WhatsApp or Telegram contact posing as a broker's research desk, offering tips or an "institutional" app, then taking deposits. A caller who can quote your real holdings and your PAN is far more persuasive than one guessing, and this leak supplies exactly that. Note the dates too.

The breach happened in April 2023 and was confirmed in July 2024, more than a year later. The data had plenty of time to circulate before anyone was told. If you held an Angel One account in that period, treat any unsolicited contact about your portfolio as fraudulent unless you started it, and never move money to an account a caller gives you, however much they know.

The record's three dates tell the story in order: the breach in April 2023, the confirmation in July 2024, and the addition to HIBP in October 2026. Each step happened long after the previous one, and an account holder checking today is looking at data that has been usable for more than three years.

Portfolio holdings change, but a PAN, a bank account number and a home address mostly do not, so age reduces the value of this data much less than it would for a password list. Market regulators in India publish warnings about unregistered investment advisers and fake trading apps, and the safest habit is to check any adviser or platform against the regulator's own register before engaging.

Brokers do not run stock-tip groups on messaging apps or ask clients to install a separate app to receive "institutional" allocations. If you were contacted by someone who knew your holdings, report it to the broker through its official support channel, and do not continue the conversation where it started.

fields.name: Government issued IDs
fields.why: Passport and licence numbers are used to prove identity to banks and telecoms, and they are effectively permanent.

fields.name: Bank account numbers
fields.why: Enables direct-debit fraud and gives a caller the detail needed to sound like the bank.

fields.name: Physical addresses
fields.why: Where someone actually lives. Combined with a name this moves the risk off the internet.

fields.name: Phone numbers
fields.why: Enables SIM-swap attacks against SMS two-factor codes, and puts the number on scam-call lists indefinitely.

fields.name: Dates of birth
fields.why: One of the three things call centres ask to verify identity, and it never changes.

fields.name: Names
fields.why: Turns an anonymous address into an identified person, which is what makes targeted phishing possible.

fields.name: Email addresses
fields.why: An exposed address may be used in phishing attempts. Treat unexpected messages with caution.

fields.name: Financial investments
fields.why: Adds detail to a profile that can be assembled from several breaches at once.

actions: Move two-factor authentication off SMS and onto an authenticator app, which a SIM swap cannot intercept.
Check statements for the months after the breach date and ask your bank for a replacement card if the number was full.
Consider a credit freeze. A government identifier cannot be changed, so limiting what can be opened in your name is the only real control.
Be sceptical of post and callers who already know your address, knowing it is no longer evidence of anything.
Be alert to phishing. A message may use details from exposed or collected records to appear familiar; verify requests through the service directly.
breach.scale_line: The address count is about 25% of the population of Australia.
